youtube_title: Cashing a 'Payment in Full' Check Can Settle a Disputed Bill
caption: Under UCC 3-311 (Nebraska's version shown), a good-faith check clearly offered as full payment of a genuinely disputed claim can settle it once cashed — with exceptions for designated addresses and repayment within 90 days.
script: Write three words on a check, and you might legally wipe out the rest of a bill you're fighting. [disclaimer] Meet Gary. Gary hired a contractor to fix his deck. The contractor sends a bill for two thousand dollars. But Gary honestly thinks the work was bad. So Gary sends a check for fifteen hundred. And he writes on it, payment in full. It's a real rule in American business law. It's called accord and satisfaction. Nebraska's version is a good example. If there's no real fight and you just owe the bill, it doesn't work. Companies can set a special address for these checks. And they can often undo it by paying the money back within ninety days. script_old: Cashing a check can sometimes settle a disputed bill, even when the check is for less. This comes from the Uniform Commercial Code, section three-three-eleven. Nebraska's version is a good example. It's called accord and satisfaction. Here's how it works. First, there has to be a genuine dispute about the amount owed, or an amount that isn't fixed. Second, the person paying offers a check in good faith, as full satisfaction of the claim. Third, the check, or a letter with it, has to clearly and conspicuously say it's offered as full payment. And fourth, the person who's owed money cashes it. Then the claim can be discharged. Picture a hypothetical. A contractor bills two thousand dollars. The customer honestly disputes the work, and sends a check for fifteen hundred, clearly marked as payment in full. If the contractor cashes it, the dispute may be over. But writing payment in full isn't magic. If there's no real dispute, and you simply owe the bill, it doesn't work. Companies can designate a special address for these checks, and if yours doesn't go there, the discharge may fail.
